Android Auto Is Acting Up Again, and at This Point, I Am Too Afraid To Install New Updates
6 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution/Google
Yes, you’ve heard it right. Android Auto is acting up again, and this time, it also broke down the wireless connection in my car. It all happened after the installation of Android Auto 17.6, an update served through the Google Play Store as an automatic release.
Needless to say, I didn’t change anything on my side, and the configuration that worked just fine before the update is now broken after I installed the new version.
My Skoda Kodiaq is fitted with factory-installed Android Auto wired and wireless support, and I use both versions depending on where I’m going. For short drives, I rely on Android Auto wireless for the added convenience. For a longer drive, I plug in my Google Pixel 10 Pro XL because the battery impact would otherwise be significant.
However, after I installed Android Auto 17.6, neither of the two connects. I plug in my phone, and despite it starting to charge - once again, I didn’t change anything on my side, so I still use the cable that worked flawlessly before the update - Android Auto no longer fires up. I tried all the typical workarounds, including the usual cache cleaning.
After giving a try to all these fixes that don’t typically help much, I decided to remove the phone profile from the car and re-pair the mobile device with the vehicle. It worked, with Android Auto wired now launching correctly. The wireless connection was still broken, and no matter what I did, Android Auto still shut down when I removed the cable.
The next time I got in my car, boom, the same thing again. Android Auto refused to launch, and the only thing that got it up and running again was the same trick I detailed above. Needless to say, re-pairing my phone with my car every time I need to go somewhere isn’t the most convenient thing, so I started searching the web for fixes.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution It turns out I’m not the only one struggling with a similar problem. A discussion thread that was started on Google’s forums earlier this week describes a similar problem. It also happens in a Skoda (also a Kodiaq), but this time the phone involved is a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The issue happens with factory Android Auto wireless.
The OP complains that Android Auto no longer works after the engine is shut down, and the only workaround is to re-pair the phone with the vehicle.
“The only fix is to forget the car on the phone (and delete the phone on the car's infotainment), then go through the whole pairing process again. After that, it works again until the next time I stop and turn the engine off,” the poster explains.
Several users stepped in and confirmed the same behavior in their cars, but someone says that Android Auto wired still works properly even when wireless is broken. This doesn’t happen in my case, as both wired and wireless appear to be unavailable when the glitch is triggered.
Oddly, one of the things I tried was a downgrade to an earlier version, but Android Auto continued to malfunction in the same way.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Other Skoda owners complain both on Google’s forums and on reddit - and it appears that owners of other cars in the Volkswagen group are struggling with a similar experience - that Android Auto is lagging and feels extremely slow after the update.
“At some point during the trip, navigation starts lagging behind, touch is very slow to react, and after some time, the whole screen gets blurry. This happens in multiple navigation software (at least Waze and Google Maps) [and] across multiple cars and different types of phones (Google Pixel, Samsung, OnePlus),” someone explains on Google’s forums.
No workaround is available in this case, despite someone explaining that updating to Android Auto 17.7 brought things back to normal.
I also installed the latest versions manually on my Google Pixel - including the recently-released Android Auto 18.0 beta - and the problems persist. The only thing that brings things back to normal is removing the phone profile and re-paring the devices from scratch every time I turn on the engine.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution At this point, I’m already afraid to install new Android Auto versions, especially when everything is working as expected. A perfectly running configuration can end up struggling with these kinds of bugs without us changing anything, so maybe Google should pay a little bit more attention to the testing phase before giving the go-ahead for production builds.
I’ve always avoided installing beta builds on my main phone, specifically because I use Android Auto as a daily driver, so stability and reliability are critical for me.
I’m still waiting for a fix, so if you somehow came across similar problems in your Skoda or Volkswagen, make sure you drop me a comment in the box below. A fix would be greatly appreciated.

The Mazda CX-30's 2027 Update Expands UK Range From 17 to 21 Versions
16 photos
Photo: Mazda
Over in the United Kingdom, prospective customers now have more ways to spend money on the CX-30. Even though Mazda has not made any mechanical changes to the front-biased crossover, it did grow the UK range to a grand total of 21 versions for model year 2027.
Under the hood, buyers are presented with a choice between 140 or 186 metric ponies of e-Skyactiv G or e-Skyactiv X muscle. That's 138 and 183 mechanical horsepower, respectively, and only e-Skyactiv X specifications can be furthered with all-wheel drive. In this case, i-Activ stands for an electronically controlled system that comes in the form of a power transfer unit.
Said all-wheel-drive setup favors 2WD operation, leaving the front wheels do the talking for most of the time in order to save fuel. The rear coupling, meanwhile, does its job under hard acceleration, spirited cornering, and when front slip is detected. Mazda says the system can predict a traction shortfall, responding more aggressively if the front wheels do slip.
Only the base Prime Line trim level is available with either a manual or an automatic. Everything else comes with the six-speed automatic exclusively. Customers who prefer the more interesting route should go for the e-Skyactiv X, which switches between compression and spark ignition depending on load. The X and G families of engines will be ultimately discontinued by the Skyactiv Z family, whose party trick is a Lambda 1.0 air-fuel ratio across a wider load band.
New for 2027 in the United Kingdom, the Homura Plus grade slots above Homura and builds on said version's blacked-out exterior treatment. Additions include black leather upholstery, 12-speaker Bose audio, power-adjustable front seats, upgraded LED lighting, gunmetal and gloss-black interior trim, and a 360-degree camera system.
Photo: Mazda The headlight addition for 2027, however, is ventilation for the front seats. A CX-30 first, it does sound minor until you remember how much of this crossover segment is decided by how much equipment can be crammed in such a small package. Cooled front seats give Mazda a concrete answer to increasingly more competitive alternatives, and the Homura Plus further sweetens the deal with a heating function.
Homura customers, on the other hand, are presented with a bit of a visual makeover. The beltline moldings, grille surround wing, roof rails, and all exterior badging go black, giving this grade a darker look that leans into the sporty lines of the CX-30. The Exclusive-Line and Takumi take the opposite route, boasting silver for their beltline trim pieces, grille surround wing, roof rails, and badging. Takumi remains the flagship, and it gains a 360-degree camera for model year 2027.
See-Through View mode allows the driver to see around obstacles ahead of the car while maneuvering, which should come in handy in a variety of scenarios. Think of it as an upgraded surround-view system designed to reveal hazards around the vehicle when parking or maneuvering in very tight places. Entry-level buyers haven't been forgotten either, for the Prime-Line gains enhanced Smart Brake Support and Blind Spot Monitoring.
The latter now includes a door-opening warning for approaching traffic. Driver Monitoring is now standard across the range, while Center-Like trims move from 16-inch gray alloy wheels to an 18-inch design in silver.
Alongside Aero Gray, the color palette gains a pale green shade dubbed Zinc Green Metallic. The Makoto special edition will follow in early 2027, beautifying the CX-30 with a light cloth and stone-colored artificial leather interior. Dark-plated badging, a black front signature wing, black alloys, and black mirror caps complete the Makoto's visual theme.

Apple Maps Gets DCE Update As There's Basically No Reason To Dump Google Maps
6 photos
Photo: Apple Maps
I wouldn’t blame anyone for thinking that Apple has abandoned the Detailed City Experience . Updates on this front have landed at a frustratingly slow pace, but the iPhone maker has just dropped another refresh supposed to remind us that Apple Maps is still around.
The DCE is now live in Austin, Texas, bringing the same impressive improvements as in all the other regions where the same update went live.
The detailed city experience includes highly detailed maps with sidewalks, crosswalks, trees, 3D buildings, and elevation. Apple is paying particular attention to landmarks, creating high-resolution 3D models that almost perfectly resemble the real-life versions. In Austin, you can explore the Texas State Capitol, the Moody Center, the Blanton Museum of Art, and the Darrell K Royal Texas Memorial Stadium.
Apple sometimes adds new 3D models, so the maps could get more details in the coming months. Most often, these updates go live silently, so the only way to spot them is to check back again in a while.
Photo: Apple Maps The slow Detailed City Experience rollout Apple started the DCE rollout in 2021, but only a dozen locations have received it so far. The focus was mostly on American updates, whereas users in Europe received the new maps in very limited locations, such as Amsterdam, Hamburg, London, and Paris.
Everybody expected the DCE to be a global update whose broad availability would be reached shortly after the announcement. But five years later, the DCE is still unavailable for most users, with updates going live at a very slow pace.
There’s a good reason why so many users - those who are running Apple Maps, at least - want the DCE. With this update, Apple Maps is getting not only the new maps, but also improved navigation, including on CarPlay. Apple Maps essentially becomes a solid Google Maps alternative in those regions where the DCE is available.
Photo: Apple Maps Google’s response But while Apple is rolling out the DCE at a pace that makes people forget about the update - at one point, the company needed over 300 days to release a DCE update - Google is moving at a much faster pace.
Google has already announced a similar update for Google Maps. It’s called immersive navigation and includes the same highly detailed experience as in the Apple Maps DCE.
With immersive navigation , Google is putting the focus on terrain details and improved visuals, with Gemini powering more detailed turn-by-turn guidance and offering more context when helping drivers reach a specific destination. Instead of a simple “turn right” instruction, Gemini can check out the map and offer more detailed information, including landmarks and buildings, to make it easier for drivers to figure out where they need to make the turn.
Photo: Apple Maps The new maps also focus on 3D visuals, though this isn’t necessarily a surprise. Google has been exploring this side of Google Maps with immersive view and immersive view for routes, which uses data from multiple sources, including aerial shots, historic traffic data, and Street View imagery, to create a digital version of a specific region.
The improved Google Maps experience is already live in the United States, and Google plans to bring it to the rest of the world in the coming month. The update involves a lot of work, just like in the case of the Apple Maps DCE, but Google seems to be a lot more committed to updating all regions to the new immersive experience.
Apple’s commitment to Apple Maps While Apple still sees Apple Maps as an essential part of its service arsenal, the commitment to rolling out major improvements to the platform appears to have changed after the iPhone maker allegedly abandoned the development of the Apple Car .
Apple Car played a key role in the project, as it was originally supposed to power the self-driving capabilities of the vehicle. Once Apple stopped working on an Apple Car, everybody expected the company to focus significantly more on software and services, including Apple Maps and CarPlay.
Photo: Apple Maps However, the slow DCE rollout continued, and Apple Maps barely received any significant improvements. Apple also released a web version of Apple Maps, but it lacked and still lacks essential functionality, including the ability to log in with an Apple ID.
Apple Maps continues to be a solid navigation app for users in the United States, while for reviews and business information, Google Maps still appears to be the best option. For everybody else living in non-US regions, Google Maps continues to serve as the preferred mapping platform, at least until Apple accelerates the rollout of the detailed city experience to bring the new maps to more users.
You can see the new detailed city experience in Austin, Texas, in Apple Maps today on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac. The new maps are already there for all Apple users, including the 3D landmarks that I highlighted in the gallery here.

Nissan Altima Refuses to Die, the 2027 Model Year of the Classic Mid-Sizer Kicks Off at $27,790
6 photos
Photo: Nissan
Surprisingly, the Japanese automaker's local division in America hasn't retired the traditional Nissan Altima, but it now costs a little more - $29,065 with destination and handling included ($1,275).
The average transaction price (ATP) for a new vehicle in the United States was $50,562 in September 2026, according to data from Kelley Blue Book, which is up almost one percentage point from August and up 0.7% year-over-year. That’s immediately below the current all-time record of $50,614 set in December 2025.
Clearly, the market continues to absorb inflation and go up, but what that means is that many customers don’t have enough options below that threshold anymore. So, let’s applaud the fact that a carmaker hasn’t killed off another affordable option and that the 2027 Nissan Altima refuses to die and sees another model year, at least.
Even with the DFC included, the starting price remains below the $30k threshold. On the other hand, the bad news is that, just like it happened with the 2027 Toyota Camry, a direct competitor, things continue to get worse in terms of starting MSRPs because the 2027 Altima is more expensive than its predecessor. Also, the options are shrinking – gone is the all-wheel-drive option on the entry-level SV trim.
The 2027 Nissan Altima, which competes in the same (shrinking) segment as the ultra-popular 2027 Toyota Camry along with other foes like the Honda Accord, Hyundai Sonata, and Kia K5, has been rumored to end its career after the 2026 model year. The automaker has now announced the 2027 model year is alive and well, albeit with slightly higher price tags.
Nissan still has the 2027 Sentra starting from $22,990 (sans destination) and the 2026 Altima used to kick off at $27,580 for the base SV model, which had both FWD and AWD. Now it’s $27,790 sans DFC, and only FWD is available. Also gone are the SV Special Edition along with the SR Midnight Edition. Also, the 2026 Altima SR used to start at $28,980, but now it’s $29,190 with FWD and $30,690 with AWD, plus $1,275 for destination and handling.
Luckily, the price differences aren’t huge, and both the 2027 Altima SV and SR “offer a range of comfort, convenience and safety features that enhance the driving experience, including the reassurance of standard Nissan Safety Shield 360, class-exclusive Intelligent Forward Collision Warning, and available ProPILOT Assist for more convenient highway driving.”
The Nissan Altima also has “class-exclusive Zero Gravity seats,” standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, optional wireless phone charging, an available 12.3-inch touchscreen infotainment system, and standard Remote Engine Start. The Altima SR goes towards a sporty lifestyle with 19-inch alloy wheels, gloss black exterior trim, carbon fiber center console trim and sports exhaust finishers.
There are also standard paddle shifters, Active Ride Control, Intelligent Trace Control and sport suspension (FWD models only). All versions have the same 2.5-liter direct-injection engine rated for 188 horsepower (182 hp with AWD). Front-wheel drive models get fuel economy ratings of up to 26 mpg city and 36 mpg highway.

Tesla's China-Built Model 3 Premium Exhausts Canadian Import Quota
20 photos
Photo: Tesla
The automaker that made electric vehicles cool has recently stopped taking orders for the Shanghai-made Model 3 in Canada, and the reason is not collapsing demand for the more aerodynamic brother of the Model Y. Instead, the American manufacturer was forced to pull the plug due to the federal import quota for China-made electric vehicles.
Tesla posted a notice in this regard back on October 12, claiming that high demand for the cheaper Model 3 had exhausted its allocation. Orders should resume in March 2027 as the suits in Ottawa issue more capacity for automakers who source their vehicles from China.
This pause covers both the rear-drive Premium and the all-wheel-drive version, which retail at CAD 39,490 and CAD 49,990, respectively. The starting price actually stands at CAD 42,132 after including the delivery and other fees. As one of Canada's most affordable new EVs, the Model 3 Premium has been a hugely successful product in said part of the world.
The Model 3 Premium from China wouldn't have been this commercially successful had Ottawa not replaced its 100 percent levy on Chinese battery-electric vehicles with an annual tariff-rate quota. Under this arrangement, Canada allows up to 49,000 electric vehicles from China each year at a most-favored-nation tariff of merely 6.1 percent.
Tesla resumed shipments of the Chinese Model 3 in May, and the result was a dramatic rebound after a less-than-stellar 2025. As per Automotive News, the brand's Canadian sales fell 63.5 percent last year. The lower-cost Premium from China helped pull the company back. Unfortunately, exact Canadian sales figures remain unknown for the time being.
Photo: Tesla Although Tesla says the quota is gone, that is not completely true. Citing a Global Affairs Canada's Export and Import Controls System report, Automotive News learned that only 15,931 permits have been issued or used against the 49,000-vehicle ceiling for the first year of the quota system. That leaves 33,069 permits on the table, roughly two-thirds of the first quota year.
In other words, there is a clear distinction between a manufacturer's allocation and the national ceiling. Per the cited publication, most permits are presumed to have gone to Tesla. Automakers who have also used this system to bring Chinese electric vehicles to Canada include Geely-controlled Polestar and Lotus, and the Ford Motor Company's Lincoln brand has also secured permits for the Nautilus.
The first six-month window of the program saw 24,500 permits become available, of which 15,603 were claimed. The second window kicked off back on September 1, carrying over 8,897 unused permits. As of October 9, it's understood that only 328 vehicles had entered Canada under that second window. Given the aforementioned, it appears that Ottawa needs to optimize remaining quota availability.
Canada's first quota year runs through February 2027, with the annual allowance resetting on March 1, 2027. The second quota year sees the annual allowance rise to 52,185 vehicles nationwide, giving Tesla and other companies a fresh pool of import capacity. As long as they secure allocations, of course.
Vehicles sold in Canada under this system have to meet Canadian motor vehicle safety standards, which means that newcomers from China like Geely need regulatory approval to receive allocations. While Tesla may have an established sales network and proven products, Chinese brands have the upper hand in terms of pricing and model variety. These advantages could very well hurt Tesla and other legacy automakers in the long run.
Via // Automotive News

source_document.body:
The AI boom has created insatiable demand for high-performance computing, driving up the cost on everything from GPUs and CPUs to high-bandwidth memory and even networking. The boom has triggered a real-estate frenzy, driven up power costs, and even has people worried about water shortages. But it’s also raising big questions about AI itself, such as: Will it ever actually pay off?
The industry keeps racking up milestones thanks to generative AI. For instance, the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) announced last week that we’ve already reached $1 trillion in chip sales for the calendar year. It’s the first time in history that chip sales have reached 12 digits–and it only took eight months. Global chip sales for August grew at a ridiculous 144.3% clip–180.9% in the Americas–and we’ll likely end the year with $1.6 trillion in sales, says Michael Robbins, SIA president and CEO.
Chip sales are skyrocketing (Source: SIA)
Growth in chip sales normally follows a somewhat predictable curve, thanks to the massive, multi-year investments required to build chip fabs. Clearly, profits are taking up a big chunk of the area under the sharp, elbow-like curve that SIA shared, as the inputs for chips themselves haven’t changed much. The difference is the absurd level of demand for silicon, caused by AI.
SIA’s data jibes with the latest out of Gartner , which in late September announced its prediction that worldwide spending on AI would total $2.7 trillion in 2026, a 49.5% increase in just one year, with another 36% leap expected in 2027 to $3.6 trillion (this is just for AI, not for keeping the ERP system running).
As Gartner analyst John-David Lovelock pointed out: “The buildout of AI data center capacity is the largest infrastructure project humanity has even undertaken.”
Now, humans have built big projects over the past 5,000 years. Egyptians moved 6 million tons of block to build the Great Pyramids of Giza, the Chinese constructed a 13,000-mile fortification called the Great Wall, and the US laid down 49,000 miles of pavement for the Interstate Highway System.
All of these multi-year projects took massive amounts of capital as well as human labor to build. The AI boom, which is currently in its fourth year, makes previous mega-projects look like child’s play, according to a new paper titled “ Financing the AI Buildout ,” by Stinj Van Nieuwerburgh, a professor of real estate and finance at the Columbia Business School.
“Relative to the economy, the projected buildout would exceed the major U.S. canal, railroad, electrification, highway, and telecommunications investment booms,” Van Nieuwerburgh writes.
Source: “Financing the AI Buildout,” by Stinj Van Nieuwerburgh
Van Nieuwerburgh estimates that a single 200 megawatt AI data center will cost about $8.2 billion to build, with two-thirds of that amount going to outfit it with IT gear (servers, switches, networking, cooling) and one-third to buy real-estate and electrical connections.
“We estimate that 188 GW of new capacity will be completed during 2025–2032, with a further 115 GW completed after 2032,” he writes. “This pipeline generates approximately $9.0 trillion in investment during 2025–2032, averaging 3.22 percent of [U.S.] GDP per year.”
So where is all the money to finance this AI blowout coming from? And how will the AI applications running on all that HPC actually generate a return for the investors?
Hyperscalers like Amazon , Microsoft , Alphabet , and Meta –collectively worth $13 trillion in market cap–are doing a lot of the heavy lifting, Van Nieuwerburgh points out. These companies have increased their capital expenditures from about $97 billion in 2020 to more than $400 billion in 2025, a number that’s expected to double to $800 billion this year.
Since these figures exceed the company’s operating cash, the hyperscalers are bringing in external partners to help provide capital for the investments. There is a raft of “data center developers, infrastructure funds, REITs, and private equity investors” who are providing cash, while another group composed of banks, private credit funds, and securitization vehicles supply debt to finance construction of the nearly 200 GW of data center capacity expected over the next five years, according to Van Nieuwerburgh.
Source: “Financing the AI Buildout,” by Stinj Van Nieuwerburgh
Just as developers historically have looked to spread out the risk inherent in large-scale capital projects such as construction of buildings and electrical infrastructure, the AI boom is giving us new structures for handling the risks with buying hundreds of billions of dollars of GPUs.
“Investment-grade hyperscaler tenants make these structures financeable by supporting long-duration contractual cash flows, while frontier AI firms effectively access infrastructure through the hyperscalers’ balance sheets and creditworthiness,” Van Nieuwerburgh writes.
However, these arrangements don’t eliminate risk, he writes–they merely transform it. And potentially, they can amplify it.
“Long-duration debt is then supported by cash flows and collateral values that depend on uncertain AI demand, rapid technological change, timely access to power and hardware, and the continued credit quality of a small number of tenants,” Van Nieuwerburgh writes. “The resulting capital structure can therefore make exposures more layered, correlated, and difficult to observe.”
It does not appear that Van Nieuwerburgh is trying to be an alarmist in his paper. Rather, he sees the events as a worthwhile laboratory to study “how modern economies finance a general-purpose technology in real time.”
Stinj Van Nieuwerburgh of Columbia Business School
His study is also valuable because it lays out the underlying facts of the AI boom in great detail. For instance, his estimate of the IT costs illustrate the scale of the investments being made. At 142 kW per rack, one could install 1,170 GB300 NVL72 systems at $4.0 million each, or $4.68 billion in total, into a typical 200 megawatt data center. “This price already includes the GPUs, attached highbandwidth memory, Grace CPUs, NVLink switching, power systems, and the physical rack,” Van Nieuwerburgh writes. “We add 10 percent of the rack cost for the external network fabric and fiber, 5 percent for shared storage, and 5 percent for cluster-level installation, integration, and commissioning.” Sounds about right.
The AI boom is many things. It has enormous potential for scientific discovery, as we have explored in HPCwire pages. It’s a technological revolution, reshaping the trillion-dollar IT industry in its image. It’s upending business processes and giving new meaning to workflow automation. For some, it represents a new form of entertainment, or even a new digital form of life–and potentially threatening our own lives. It’s an engine of growth for millions of peoples’ 401(k)s and is making a much smaller group of individuals ludicrously wealthy.
AI is all of these things. But at the end of the day, AI will need to show a return on the investment, or the investments will slow. We know that $9.0 trillion is slated to be invested over the next five years, although who exactly holds the risk is somewhat vague, as Van Nieuwerburgh shows us.
Will the payoff for AI ever reach $9 trillion? That ultimately is AI’s big question.
